rv.q: It’s a compelling reading of Shakespeare’s play, even if it loses its way when its deathtoll climbs.
So, a well-put together, beautifully choreographed production but one with a frustrating emotional vacuum at its centre.
Hastie just doesn’t bring the rigour to bear to make this a classic production - you have to be incredibly meticulous to carry off anarchy in a Shakespeare play.
Hastie’s interpretation is full of novel ideas and subtly revelatory touches but feels ponderous and staid overall.
And this is an oddly uneven Hamlet, strangely lacking in tension and weight.
If only the rest of the evening pulsed with such ingenuity.
Robert Hastie's production looks fabulous on Ben Stones's handsome set of a palatial ballroom with dado-to-ceiling frescoes illustrating Danish military history.
At the National Theatre, it feels below par.

Leaning into every opportunity for unsettling humour, but neglecting the rich emotional depth that can make Shakespeare’s tragic masterpiece so powerful, this latest take on the classic tale of delayed revenge is flat, hollow and unfocused.
For all his charisma, the evening winds up fast-paced but fatally unmoving.
So we’re left with a fitful evening that lurches from one lush tableau to another.
Challenging, entertaining, and compelling, it takes one of the most well-known plays in the English language and shows us something new.
Francesca Mills presents an Ophelia like none I’ve ever seen.
Like all the best versions of the tale, this production of Hamlet manages to fit into each one of those boxes.
Hastie has provided a handsome, clear-sighted production. But it's Mills who provides its heart.
Even with all the stylistic flourish, my bet is this won’t be a Hamlet for the National’s history books.
What a pity, then, that this promise peters out, and an ambitious conceit ultimately fails to deliver.
This is a flat-share Hamlet without depth or intellectual curiosity.
Yet there is something about this production which maintains interest, even over an almost three-hour running time.
“A hit? A palpable hit?” No, not in this incarnation and Denmark became a prison for me.

cn.t: Abeysekera brings manic energy to Hamlet in Hastie's visually striking but uneven production. Critics praise the inventive staging and Mills' standout Ophelia, but fault the rushed, comedic approach for sacrificing emotional depth.
